title: Nucleus overload guide (part. 3): my experience & sports applications
summary: Final part of his nucleus overload (NO) guide: he details which body parts he currently trains with high-volume, high-frequency, low-intensity work (calves, lats, rear delts, traps, neck, triceps, forearms) and which he doesn't, recounts past accidental NO (daily heavy cheat curls, daily hour-long ab sessions, scoliosis-driven asymmetries), and explains why athletes and manual workers show NO-like development but why bodybuilders still need high intensity to save time.

claims.claim: His nucleus overload runs a high-volume, high-frequency, low-intensity protocol on nearly every body part he wants to grow, mostly with isolation movements rather than heavy compounds.
Calves NO: single-leg calf raises with very light weight (~10 lbs) every two days, 70-100 reps per leg, alongside separate heavy progressed calf work.
He does no NO for quads since they're big enough; heavy, high-intensity, low-volume squats suffice.
Hamstrings are his fastest-growing muscle but not a good candidate for NO; he trains them only with heavy deadlifts and hip hinges. Glutes, lower back and rhomboids likewise only get compounds.
Lats NO: light high-rep pullovers every two days and 40-100 bodyweight pull-ups every day except Sundays; both stretch the lats a lot and are easy to recover from.
For NO to work you must connect well with the exercise and be able to repeat it again and again; stretch-heavy, easy-to-recover movements are ideal.
Rear delts and traps are his most lacking muscles; he does 40 to 200 band face pulls every day with varying bands, plus Arnold raises, snatch-grip pulls and lateral raises.
Traps are the easiest muscle to apply NO to and respond very fast; use weighted stretches with near-maximal weight, staying healthy. Traps are very resistant and practically can't be torn.
He does about 150 shrugs with varying weights after every pull, deadlift or lower-body session, ending heavy sets with a loaded forward stretch held until his upper back rounds.
Neck NO: neck curls every day with low weight and high volume, sometimes high weight and low volume; he considers this the best way to grow the neck, with plates/harness stalling at some point.
He keeps biceps on high-intensity low-volume work only because more growth would dwarf his triceps.

He prioritizes the triceps long head for the double biceps pose: heavy skull crushers plus band extensions behind and in front of the head every two days, done on deadlift/squat days or arm day, never on bench days when triceps are needed to press.
Forearm NO is doable but risky because fatigued forearms weaken grip for curls and other work.
Bodybuilders have no reason to deadlift with hook or mixed grip; pull double overhand or with straps.
His forearm NO is grippers, dead hangs with various grips including towel, and towel pull-ups; dynamic wrist curls are done as normal strength training.
Dead hangs may be underrated for arm growth because of the stretch they put on the arms, e.g. the triceps, not just the lats.
Every body part under NO must also get heavy weights; chasing pump with low intensity alone doesn't work for naturals.
His big biceps came from daily heavy cheat curls, about 4 sets of 6, every day with no breaks: a high-intensity, low-volume, high-frequency form of NO that never gave him tendinitis.
You can combine two of high volume, high frequency and high intensity, but not all three; the trifecta summons injury.

As a teen obsessed with abs and biceps, he did full-ROM sit-ups (sometimes with a plate) for 45-60 minutes every day, once even after vomiting with stomach flu at football practice; his abs and obliques remain very developed.
Muscles trained with NO tend to stay leaner and more vascular, and gains are retained and come back more easily.
You won't lose NO gains when you stop: his biceps went from daily to every 4 days without shrinking, and his abs from 45 min/day to under 10 min/week with no loss.

A muscle used to a certain tonnage won't regress as long as it gets challenging weight; tonnage accumulated at low intensity can be maintained with lower total tonnage at high intensity, showing not all tonnage is equal.
Don't run NO in cycles; run it until you like how the muscle looks, then move to a new project.

Because of scoliosis his left shoulder sits higher; two years of mixed-grip deadlifts stretching his supinated arm made that biceps visibly bigger, showing the power of weighted stretch, though such static stretch also risks a biceps tear.
Scoliosis made one shoulder do more work on bench, and that side's front delt is fuller; limb-length differences can cause similar asymmetries.

Manual workers show NO-like development: laborers carrying loads all day, welders with big forearms after 20 years, arm wrestlers with oversized forearms and biceps, bike couriers with developed calves.
High-volume high-frequency activity in youth may increase myonuclei so much that it stays visible for life (he links it to epigenetics).
Athletes show NO effects: ballerinas have huge calves at ~110 lbs, swimmers have massive shoulders and lats.

Athletes get that development as a byproduct of ~8 hours of daily training; bodybuilders don't have that time, which is why they need high intensity. NO for every body part would take 10 hours in the gym.
